question.text: Sunita has a retirement corpus of Rs. 1 crore. Assume a fixed monthly portfolio return of 10% p.a. compounded monthly, with no volatility, taxes, fees, or inflation. She starts a Systematic Withdrawal Plan (SWP) of Rs. 70,000 per month. Under these simplifying assumptions, how long will her corpus last?

answer.text: The corpus will sustain indefinitely as the assumed monthly portfolio return exceeds the withdrawal

explanation.text: The Logic: Under the stated assumption of a fixed 10% p.a. monthly return, the assumed monthly portfolio return on Rs. 1,00,00,000 is Rs. 1,00,00,000 x (10%/12) = Rs. 83,333. Since this exceeds the monthly withdrawal of Rs. 70,000, the corpus does not deplete — it grows by approximately Rs. 13,333 each month before further compounding. The annuity depletion formula collapses to an indefinite horizon because the effective net withdrawal is negative. The Trap: Candidates often rush into the annuity-depletion formula without first checking whether the assumed monthly return covers the withdrawal. If it does, the formula's logarithm becomes undefined, signalling that under the simplifying assumption the corpus is sustainable indefinitely. Note: The workbook is explicit that an SWP is NOT equivalent to monthly interest from a fixed deposit — each payout redeems units, and real-world returns vary. This question deliberately states a fixed-return assumption so the answer can be computed; in practice, volatility, taxes and inflation must all be modelled separately.
